bullets: How temperature, heat and the gas laws fit together: kinetic theory, conduction, convection and radiation
slides.heading: JC H2 physics — thermal: kinetic theory, gas laws and temperature
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we treat a gas as a swarm of molecules in random motion, and by the end you will be able to connect temperature to average kinetic energy, use the gas laws, and explain all three heat-transfer mechanisms without falling for the every-molecule-faster trap.

bullets: State that temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules, and use the ideal-gas law pV = nRT
Explain conduction, convection and radiation at the particle level, and use radiated power growing as T^4
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting why a hotter gas still has some slow molecules.

bullets: A small cup of water at 80 degrees holds less total heat than a big bucket at 30 degrees
Temperature and heat are not the same thing - one is an average, the other is a total
slides.heading: A tiny hot cup versus a big warm bucket
slides.notes: Show the two containers and ask: which is hotter, and which holds more heat? Take two or three answers, then say: hold both answers, because by the misconception scene you will see they can point in opposite directions.

bullets: Temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules: average KE = (3/2) k T, with T in kelvin
Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules
An ideal gas obeys pV = nRT: at fixed volume, pressure is proportional to the kelvin temperature
slides.heading: Temperature is an average, heat is a total
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: temperature averages the molecules, heat and internal energy add them up, and the gas laws are what the swarm does when you squeeze it or heat it.

bullets: The same four molecules jiggle harder as the dial turns from 300 K to 450 K to 600 K
Nothing else changes: hotter means a higher average kinetic energy, molecule by molecule on average
slides.heading: Temperature: molecules jiggle faster when hotter
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the jitter grow as the needle turns - the molecules are the same, the box is the same, only the average kinetic energy has risen.

bullets: Atoms at the hot end jiggle hard and bump their neighbours, which bump theirs
In metals, free electrons carry the energy much faster than the lattice vibrations alone
slides.heading: Conduction: heat travels atom by atom
slides.notes: Follow the energy packet down the rod: no atom travels the length of the rod - each one only passes the jiggle to the next, and that relay is conduction.

bullets: Fluid warmed at the bottom expands, becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, so the loop keeps turning
slides.heading: Convection: the fluid loops
slides.notes: Trace one parcel around the tank: up the warm side, across the top, down the cool side. Convection needs a fluid that can flow - it is the bulk movement itself that carries the heat.

bullets: Every body radiates energy packets; heating the filament from 300 K to 600 K makes them come thicker and faster
Radiated power follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law P = sigma A T^4: doubling T multiplies the power by 16
slides.heading: Radiation: hotter means more packets, faster
slides.notes: Watch the power bar climb as the temperature doubles: radiation needs no medium at all, and the fourth-power law makes hot bodies dramatically brighter.

bullets: A small cup at 80 degrees has the higher temperature; the big bucket at 30 degrees holds far more total heat
Heat is the total; temperature is the average - keep the two words for the two different quantities
slides.heading: Misconception: a common mistake about heat and temperature
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the cup wins on temperature because its molecules have the higher average kinetic energy, while the bucket wins on total heat because it has so many more molecules.

bullets: Step 2: at 600 K the average doubles to 1.24 x 10^-20 J - an average over a spread of speeds, not one speed for all
slides.heading: Worked example: average kinetic energy
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: notice the answer is an average - at either temperature some molecules move far faster than this and some barely move at all.

bullets: A sealed gas at 300 K and 1.0 x 10^5 Pa is heated to 600 K at fixed volume. Find the new pressure and explain it with molecular collisions
Careful - a classmate claims: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster. Explain to them why that is wrong, and say what actually happens to the speeds
slides.heading: Your turn: averages, laws and transfers
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: the pressure doubles because the average kinetic energy doubles - but what happened to the slowest molecule in the box?

bullets: Find the pressure change when a sealed gas is heated at fixed volume, showing the kelvin temperatures
Explain why this claim is wrong: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster.
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the words average and spread of speeds in your last answer - if you can explain why some molecules still crawl in a hot gas, you have cracked today's lesson.
